architecture.r: A cluster looked fine, yet new Pods stayed pending for ten minutes. Looking at the control plane showed the scheduler was healthy but the API server was slow because etcd was on a busy disk. Knowing how the components depend on each other pointed straight at the right place.
architecture.x: Kubernetes is a set of control loops around a database. Understand which components are on the critical path, what keeps working when the control plane is down and how to size and protect etcd.

pods-and-deployments.r: A deployment replaced all Pods at once and the service was unavailable for a minute because the new Pods were not ready. Readiness probes and a rolling update with a maximum unavailable of zero kept traffic flowing.
pods-and-deployments.x: Probes, requests and update strategy decide whether a deploy is safe. Tune them from measurements, and remember that a Pod that is running is not necessarily a Pod that can serve.

services-and-ingress.r: A service could not be reached because its selector did not match the Pod labels after a rename. The service had no endpoints, which was visible at once with a single command.
services-and-ingress.x: Most connectivity problems are selector, port or policy mismatches. Check endpoints first, understand how traffic is balanced and what ingress controllers actually do with timeouts and headers.

config-and-secrets.r: A ConfigMap change did not take effect because the application read it only at startup. Mounting it as a file and restarting Pods on change, or reloading, made updates predictable.
config-and-secrets.x: Secrets in Kubernetes are only base64 by default. Encrypt them at rest, limit who can read them, prefer an external store with short-lived credentials and decide how config changes trigger rollouts.

storage.r: A Pod was rescheduled to another zone and could not attach its disk, which lived in a different zone. Using a storage class that waits for the first consumer, and spreading replicas, avoided the stuck volume.
storage.x: State changes the rules: zone affinity, access modes, expansion and backups all matter. Test restore, not only backup, and ask whether a managed service is a better home for the data.

jobs-cronjobs-daemonsets.r: A nightly job overlapped with the previous night's run after a slow day, and both wrote the same data. Setting a concurrency policy that forbids overlap and a deadline fixed it.
jobs-cronjobs-daemonsets.x: Pick the controller that matches failure semantics: retries, deadlines, overlap and cleanup. Make job work idempotent, since it will eventually run twice.

resources-and-quotas.r: A Pod kept restarting with an out-of-memory kill because its limit was lower than its real peak. Measuring actual usage and setting requests and limits from it ended the restarts and also improved scheduling.
resources-and-quotas.x: Requests drive scheduling and limits drive throttling and kills. Avoid CPU limits that cause needless throttling for latency-sensitive services, use quotas to protect shared clusters and review them as workloads change.

autoscaling.r: Traffic doubled in a minute but scaling took five, because new nodes had to be created and images pulled. Keeping some headroom and scaling on a faster signal reduced the gap during spikes.
autoscaling.x: Autoscaling is a control system with delays. Understand the signals, cooldowns and limits, test with realistic spikes, and remember that scaling out does not fix a bottleneck in a shared dependency.

rbac-and-security.r: A service account with cluster-wide admin rights was used by a compromised Pod to read secrets across namespaces. Narrow roles per workload and testing with can-i would have kept the damage to a single namespace.
rbac-and-security.x: Least privilege applies to humans, controllers and workloads alike. Audit wildcards, avoid default service account tokens where not needed, and enforce pod security settings by policy.

scheduling-and-troubleshooting.r: A Pod stayed in Pending because every node had a taint it did not tolerate. The describe output said so in plain words, and adding the toleration took seconds once someone read it.
scheduling-and-troubleshooting.x: Placement rules interact: affinity, taints, spread constraints and resource requests. Test failure of a zone, and keep rules loose enough that the scheduler can still find a home.

helm-and-kustomize.r: A Helm upgrade changed a value that was set by hand during an incident, silently undoing the fix. Keeping values in version control and reviewing the rendered difference before upgrade made changes visible.
helm-and-kustomize.x: Templating adds a layer to debug. Render and diff before applying, pin chart versions, and keep values small. Choose between Helm and overlays by how much your teams need to vary.

crds-and-operators.r: An operator managing a database got stuck in a reconcile loop after a bad custom resource was applied, and it hammered the API server. Validation on the resource and rate limits in the controller stopped the loop.
crds-and-operators.x: Operators encode operational knowledge but add code you must trust, upgrade and monitor. Treat CRDs as an API with versions, and check how the operator behaves when it is down or confused.

cni-and-cluster-networking.r: Pods on one node could not reach Pods on another after a network plugin upgrade. The plugin's pods on that node were unhealthy, which explained why cross-node traffic failed but local traffic worked.
cni-and-cluster-networking.x: Cluster networking is layers of overlay, routing, NAT and policy. Know your plugin's data path, its limits on addresses and policy scale, and how it behaves during upgrades.

cluster-install-upgrade-etcd.r: A control-plane node was lost and nobody had tested the etcd backup. The backup restored, but the procedure took hours because no one had practised it. A rehearsed runbook later cut it to minutes.
cluster-install-upgrade-etcd.x: Upgrades and restores are the real operations work. Upgrade one minor version at a time, back up etcd on a schedule, test restores and know how many control-plane nodes can fail.

cka-cks-exam-strategy.r: A candidate spent too long on one hard question and ran out of time. Practising imperative commands and moving on after a fixed time per task raised the score on the next attempt.
cka-cks-exam-strategy.x: Exams reward speed and fluency in the documentation. Practise in a timed environment, build muscle memory for generators and field lookups, and treat the exam as a baseline, not the finish.

probes-metrics-and-logging.r: A liveness probe was too strict and killed healthy Pods during a slow start, turning a minor slowdown into an outage. A startup probe and a looser liveness probe fixed the loop.
probes-metrics-and-logging.x: A bad probe causes outages. Separate startup, readiness and liveness, avoid probes that depend on downstream services, and make sure the signals you export answer real operational questions.

service-mesh-and-mtls.r: A team added a mesh for mutual TLS and found latency up and new failure modes from sidecars. They kept the mesh only for the services that needed encryption and policy, and monitored sidecar health.
service-mesh-and-mtls.x: A mesh buys security and traffic control at the cost of complexity and overhead. Adopt it for a specific need, plan upgrades and certificate rotation, and understand what happens when the control plane is unavailable.

network-policies-in-practice.r: After a default deny policy was applied, a service stopped working because it needed to reach DNS. Adding an allow for DNS and testing each flow restored it, and the team kept a test suite of allowed and blocked paths.
network-policies-in-practice.x: Policy is only enforced if your network plugin supports it. Start with default deny per namespace, allow by label, test both directions and keep a record of intended flows.

statefulsets-and-running-databases.r: A team ran a database on Kubernetes and a node failure caused a long recovery because the volume had to move. They later moved the database to a managed service and used the cluster for stateless work.
statefulsets-and-running-databases.x: Running databases on Kubernetes can work, but you own failover, backups, upgrades and tuning. Ask whether the operator is mature, whether your team has the skills and whether the managed alternative is cheaper in total.

debugging-kubernetes-workloads.r: A Pod sat in ImagePullBackOff. The events named the registry error, which was an expired pull secret. Following the same order each time, from status to events to logs to the node, turned a mystery into a five-minute check.
debugging-kubernetes-workloads.x: Use the same path every time: object status, events, logs, then the node and network. Fix the cause rather than the symptom, and capture what you learn as an alert or a policy.
